verdict.rationale: ROS 2 ships its own DDS-Security/sros2 layer. It provides 'control over communications throughout the ROS graph', authentication of participants, and security enclaves that each 'encapsulate a single policy' and can be mapped to processes, users, or devices. That is a first-party, policy-based way to restrict who can participate in, and thus command or observe, robot communications. However, the evidence never shows role-based permissions an ops lead could administer, nor separate command/configure/view rights per robot, so the capability is only a low-level communication policy. Missing for 10: explicit per-topic/service/parameter allow-deny permission documentation, role abstractions for operators, per-robot command vs configure vs view distinctions, an ops-facing permission management workflow, independent or hands-on corroboration.
